title: What If Voting Were Compulsory? Australia Fines You 20 Dollars for Skipping It

scenes.text: What if skipping an election got you fined? In Australia it does, and 90 percent always turn up.
In 1922, only 59 percent of Australians voted. In 1924, a private member's bill made voting compulsory. It passed in a single day.
At the next election, in 1925, turnout jumped to 91 percent. It has never fallen below 90 since.
The penalty began at two pounds. Today it's 20 dollars, unchanged since 1984, and you can give a valid excuse instead.
Thirty-two countries have compulsory voting on paper. Only about 19 actually enforce it.
The catch: you must show up and take a ballot. What you write on it is still your business. Australians often add a sausage sizzle.

description:
What if voting were compulsory? Australia has required it in federal elections since 1924, when a private member's bill passed both houses in a single day.
Turnout rose from 59 percent in 1922 to 91 percent in 1925 and has never fallen below 90 percent since. The penalty for not voting without a valid reason is 20 dollars, unchanged since 1984. Thirty-two countries have compulsory voting laws and about 19 enforce them.

first_comment: The original two-pound fine was worth about 160 dollars in today's money; the current 20-dollar fine is about 1 percent of a week's average pay. Would you vote if it cost you 20 dollars not to? And what should we run through next?
